title: The Kingdom of Hormuz & Eastern Arabia
subtitle: c.1200–1507 · The Jewel of the Gulf, the Jabrid Bedouin State and the Horse Trade to India

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The Hormuzi kings of the strait, the Jabrid emirs of al-Hasa and the Nabhani maliks of Oman

entries.label: New Hormuz founded on Jarun island
entries.loc: Jarun island (later called Hormuz), Strait of Hormuz
entries.hint: Pressed by Mongol raids on the mainland, the kings of Hormuz moved their capital to the barren island of Jarun at the mouth of the Gulf. From this rock with no water and no soil they built the greatest trading power the Gulf had seen since Dilmun.
entries.note: The 'Shahnama-yi Turan Shah' (a Hormuzi dynastic chronicle) and the Persian historian Wassaf; J. Aubin, 'Les princes d'Ormuz du XIIIe au XVe siècle', JA (1953).

entries.label: Hormuz at its height — kings, viziers and palace coups
entries.loc: Hormuz island; suzerainty over both Gulf shores
entries.hint: At its peak Hormuz drew tribute from the coasts and islands of the whole lower Gulf — Bahrain, Qeshm, Julfar, Qalhat, Kalba. Real power often lay with the vizier, and the throne changed hands by blinding and murder as often as by inheritance.
entries.note: Aubin (1953); the Hormuzi king-list and its instability; Barbosa and later Portuguese accounts of the vizier system.

entries.label: The Usfurids and Jarwanids of al-Hasa and Qatif
entries.hint: After the Uyunids fell, the Bedouin Usfurids and then the Qatif-based Jarwanids held eastern Arabia — minor dynasties that taxed the pearl coast and the oases and quarrelled with Hormuz over Bahrain.
entries.note: Ibn Battuta names the Usfurids (Banu 'Usfur); the Jarwanids of Qatif in the Bahrani biographical literature and later Portuguese reports.

entries.label: Ajwad ibn Zamil al-Jabri
entries.loc: al-Hasa (Jabrid capital); rule reaching Najd, Bahrain and Oman
entries.hint: Under Ajwad ibn Zamil the Bedouin Jabrids built the strongest state eastern Arabia had known for centuries — holding al-Hasa, Qatif and Bahrain, raiding into Oman and Najd, and famous across Arabia for the security of the roads and the pilgrim caravans.
entries.note: Ibn Fahd's Meccan chronicle and later sources on Ajwad al-Jabri; al-Jasir's studies of the Jabrids. Ajwad died 1507.
keywords: Ajwad ibn Zamil the Bedouin Jabrids

entries.label: The Nabhani maliks of Bahla
entries.hint: In the Omani interior the Nabhani family ruled as maliks — worldly kings, not imams — from the great mud fortress of Bahla. Ibadi scholars condemned them as usurpers and periodically raised rival imams against them, but the Nabhani held on for four centuries.
entries.note: Wilkinson, 'The Imamate Tradition of Oman' (1987) on the Nabhani period; the Bahla fort and oasis wall (UNESCO, 1987).

entries.label: Hormuz as a tributary of Timurid Shiraz
entries.hint: Hormuz survived Timur's conquests by paying tribute to the governors of Fars, keeping its trade and its kings while acknowledging a Persian overlord. Formal submission was the price of commercial autonomy.
entries.note: Aubin (1953); the Hormuz–Fars tributary relationship under the Timurids and their successors.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The fall of Kish, the wars for Bahrain and the Portuguese arrival

entries.label: Hormuz destroys Kish
entries.hint: Hormuz's last serious rival for the Gulf carrying trade, the island principality of Kish, was conquered and its role absorbed. From then until the Portuguese, no other Gulf port could challenge Hormuz.
entries.note: Aubin (1953); the Hormuz–Kish rivalry and its resolution around 1330.

entries.label: Hormuzi succession wars
entries.hint: The Hormuzi throne was chronically contested: kings were blinded and deposed by brothers, sons and viziers, and rival claimants brought in Persian or Arab troops. The kingdom's wealth survived because whoever won still needed the customs house running.
entries.note: The Hormuzi dynastic chronicles; Aubin's reconstruction of the succession crises (1953).

entries.label: The Jabrid conquest of Bahrain
entries.hint: The Jabrids wrested Bahrain island and its pearl banks from Hormuz, holding it as the richest jewel of their state. Control of Awal was worth a war to every Gulf power, and the Jabrids won this round.
entries.note: Portuguese-era reports (Barbosa) noting Jabrid rule of Bahrain; al-Jasir on the Jabrid seizure.

entries.label: Nabhani maliks against the Ibadi imams
entries.hint: Ibadi scholars repeatedly elected imams — of the Banu Kharus and others — to fight the 'kingship' of the Nabhani. The interior spent much of the period in a low, grinding war between two ideas of legitimate rule.
entries.note: Wilkinson (1987); the alternation of Nabhani maliks and elected imams in the Omani chronicle tradition (al-Salimi).

entries.label: Albuquerque storms the Omani coast and besieges Hormuz
entries.hint: A Portuguese squadron under Afonso de Albuquerque sacked Qalhat, Muscat, Khor Fakkan and Julfar in a single campaign, then forced Hormuz to submit and pay tribute. The Gulf's medieval order ended in a few weeks of naval gunfire.
entries.note: 'Commentários de Afonso de Albuquerque'; the 1507 campaign along the Arabian coast. Continued in the Portuguese Gulf folio.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The tribute system of the strait, the larin coin and Jabrid road-security

entries.label: The Hormuz customs house and vassal system
entries.hint: Every port from Basra to the Indus and along the Omani coast owed Hormuz tribute or customs, collected at a great customs house on the island. Hormuz governed not territory but a toll — the right to tax everything passing through the strait.
entries.note: Portuguese descriptions of the Hormuz customs revenue (Barbosa; Albuquerque); Aubin (1953).

entries.label: The larin — the Gulf's hooked silver currency
entries.loc: minted at Lar and Hormuz; used Gulf-wide to Ceylon
entries.hint: The 'larin', a length of silver wire bent double, was struck at Lar and circulated as the standard trade money of the Gulf, spreading to India, Ceylon and the Maldives. A currency shaped for merchants who weighed rather than counted.
entries.note: Numismatic literature on the larin (Codrington; Album, 'Checklist of Islamic Coins'); its Indian Ocean circulation.

entries.label: Jabrid justice and the security of the roads
entries.hint: Ajwad al-Jabri was remembered across Arabia for imposing order on the desert — safe caravans, protected pilgrims, punished raiders. In a region where the state's core function was making movement safe, that reputation was the measure of his power.
entries.note: Ibn Fahd's Meccan annals; the Jabrid reputation for road-security in the Arabic sources (al-Jasir).

entries.label: The Ibadi case against Nabhani kingship
entries.hint: Omani scholars kept refining the doctrine that hereditary worldly rule is illegitimate and that the community must be governed by an elected imam bound by law. The Nabhani centuries sharpened Ibadi political theory precisely because they violated it.
entries.note: The Omani 'siyar' and juristic literature of the Nabhani period; Wilkinson, 'Ibâdism' (2010).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Shia scholarship in al-Ahsa, Ibadi imams in the mountains and the tomb of Bibi Maryam

entries.label: Ibn Abi Jumhur al-Ahsa'i
entries.loc: al-Ahsa; travelled to Najaf, Mashhad, Damascus
entries.hint: The most original Shia thinker eastern Arabia produced, Ibn Abi Jumhur wove together Twelver theology, Avicennan philosophy, Sufi metaphysics and Sunni hadith into a synthesis — his 'Kitab al-Mujli' — that shaped later Shia thought in Iran and India.
entries.note: Ibn Abi Jumhur al-Ahsa'i, 'Kitab al-Mujli' and 'Awali al-La'ali'; S. Schmidtke, 'Theologie, Philosophie und Mystik im zwölferschiitischen Islam des 9./15. Jahrhunderts' (2000).

entries.label: The Shia scholarly network of al-Hasa, Qatif and Bahrain
entries.hint: The eastern Arabian oases sustained a dense tradition of Twelver learning — the Al Abi Jumhur, Ibn al-Mutawwaj al-Bahrani and many others — copying texts, teaching, and linking the region to the shrine cities of Iraq. This is the deep root of Bahrain's and Qatif's religious identity.
entries.note: The Bahrani biographical dictionaries (later, e.g. al-Bahrani's 'Lu'lu'at al-Bahrayn'); Cole, IJMES 19 (1987).

entries.label: The revived Ibadi imamates
entries.hint: Against the Nabhani, Ibadi scholars raised a series of imams — some strong, most short-lived — keeping the institution and its ideal alive through four centuries of usurpation. Ibadism survived as a political theology of resistance.
entries.note: al-Salimi, 'Tuhfat al-Ayan'; Wilkinson (1987). The imams of Banu Kharus and others.

entries.label: Sufi orders and shrine devotion spread on the coast
entries.loc: Julfar, Qalhat, the Omani and eastern-Arabian coast
entries.hint: The Qadiri and other Sufi orders spread among the coastal trading and pearling towns, and the tombs of holy men became pilgrimage sites. Popular devotion took a form the austere Ibadi and Wahhabi traditions would each, later, reject.
entries.note: Evidence for coastal Sufism and ziyara in the medieval Gulf (Peterson, 'Oman's diverse society'); shrine sites at Julfar and along the Batinah.

entries.label: The mausoleum of Bibi Maryam at Qalhat
entries.hint: Bibi Maryam, who ruled the Hormuzi port of Qalhat after her husband the vizier Ayaz died, built a domed mausoleum for him that Ibn Battuta admired and that still stands — the outstanding piece of medieval architecture on the Omani coast and a monument raised by a woman in power.
entries.note: Ibn Battuta, 'Rihla', on Qalhat and 'the mosque built by a saintly woman named Bibi Maryam'; Qalhat is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2018).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Bibi Maryam's dome, the fort of Bahla and a coast furnished in Ming porcelain

entries.label: The Bibi Maryam mausoleum and the town of Qalhat
entries.hint: Qalhat was Hormuz's Omani twin — a walled town of cisterns, a bazaar and fine houses, crowned by the Bibi Maryam tomb with its (once tiled) dome. An earthquake and the Portuguese finished it; the ruins are among the best-preserved medieval townscapes in Arabia.
entries.note: Qalhat excavations (Rougeulle, French mission); UNESCO inscription (2018); Ibn Battuta's description.

entries.label: Bahla fort and the great oasis wall
entries.hint: The Nabhani stronghold of Bahla is a vast mud-brick citadel above an oasis girdled by twelve kilometres of wall. It is the largest earthen fortification in Oman and the physical expression of the Nabhani centuries.
entries.note: Bahla Fort, UNESCO World Heritage (1987); the sur (oasis wall) and its towers.

entries.label: A coast furnished in Longquan and early Ming
entries.hint: Chinese celadon and, from about 1400, blue-and-white porcelain reached the Gulf in such quantity that it became ordinary tableware in the pearling towns and was set as ornament into mosque walls and tombs. Julfar's middens are metres deep in it.
entries.note: Far Eastern ceramics from Julfar (Kennet; Sasaki), Qalhat (Rougeulle) and Bahrain; the scale of the 14th–15th century porcelain trade.

entries.label: The Hormuzi and Omani manuscript traditions
entries.hint: Hormuz's court produced Persian chronicles and poetry; al-Ahsa and Nizwa copied and composed religious and legal texts by the hundred. The Gulf was a place where books were written and reproduced, not only where they passed through in bales.
entries.note: The 'Shahnama-yi Turan Shah' and Hormuzi court literature (Aubin); the Omani and Bahrani manuscript corpora.

entries.label: Sea shanties and the pearling songs (nahham)
entries.hint: The Gulf pearling crews sang — the 'nahham' led work-songs to set the rhythm of hauling ropes and diving, and the fleets held sung competitions in port. The tradition is documented only from the 19th century but the labour that produced it runs straight back through this period.
entries.note: Gulf pearling song (fann al-nahham / fjiri); documented by 20th-century ethnomusicologists (e.g. al-Khan; Rovsing Olsen). Continuity with medieval pearling labour is inferred.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Ahmad ibn Majid of Julfar and the summit of Arab navigational science

entries.label: Ahmad ibn Majid, the Lion of the Sea
entries.hint: Born to a family of Julfar pilots, Ibn Majid wrote some forty works on navigation, above all the 'Kitab al-Fawa'id' (1490) — star altitudes, monsoon calendars, and sailing directions for the whole ocean from Sofala to China. It is the high point of the Arab science of the sea.
entries.note: Ahmad ibn Majid, 'Kitab al-Fawa'id fi usul ilm al-bahr wa'l-qawa'id'; G. R. Tibbetts, 'Arab Navigation in the Indian Ocean before the Coming of the Portuguese' (1971).

entries.label: The instruments and method of the Gulf pilot
entries.hint: Gulf navigators fixed latitude with the 'kamal' — a board and knotted cord read against a star — steered by a 32-point rose keyed to star risings, and reckoned distance in 'zam'. Ibn Majid systematised and taught this as a formal discipline.
entries.note: Tibbetts (1971); the kamal, the sidereal compass, and the zam unit as described in Ibn Majid and Sulayman al-Mahri.

entries.label: Persian and Arabic histories of the Gulf
entries.hint: Wassaf's history, the Hormuzi dynastic chronicle, Ibn Fahd's Meccan annals and the Omani Ibadi 'siyar' between them give the Gulf, for the first time since antiquity, a running historical record written from the inside.
entries.note: Wassaf, 'Tarikh-i Wassaf'; the 'Shahnama-yi Turan Shah'; Ibn Fahd; al-Salimi. Aubin (1953) synthesises the Hormuzi material.

entries.label: Ibn Abi Jumhur's philosophical synthesis
entries.hint: Ibn Abi Jumhur argued that revelation, demonstration, mystical unveiling and the traditions of both Sunni and Shia were four roads to one truth. His attempt to reconcile them was controversial in his lifetime and influential for centuries after.
entries.note: Schmidtke (2000) on Ibn Abi Jumhur; the 'Kitab al-Mujli' and its later reception in Safavid Iran.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The horse fleets to India, the customs of Hormuz and the pearls of Julfar and Bahrain

entries.label: The horse trade to India
entries.loc: Hormuz and Qalhat → Vijayanagara, the Deccan, Delhi, Bengal
entries.hint: Every year thousands of Arabian and Persian horses were shipped from Hormuz and Qalhat to the kingdoms of India, which could not breed good cavalry mounts in their climate. Wassaf reckons ten thousand horses a year to one South Indian kingdom alone, at ruinous prices.
entries.note: Marco Polo; Wassaf on the Ma'bar horse trade; Abd al-Razzaq Samarqandi at Vijayanagara (1443). Digby, 'War-Horse and Elephant in the Delhi Sultanate' (1971).

entries.label: Hormuz, the jewel of the world
entries.hint: Spices, silk, pearls, dates, indigo, slaves and horses all passed through Hormuz's market and paid its customs. A Persian saying ran: 'if the world were a ring, Hormuz would be the jewel in it.' Its wealth rested entirely on being the necessary passage.
entries.note: Barbosa, 'The Book of Duarte Barbosa'; the proverb quoted by many visitors; Aubin (1953) on the customs revenue.

entries.label: Julfar, pearling capital of the lower Gulf
entries.hint: Julfar was the great town of the Arabian coast between Bahrain and Oman — a pearling port, a horse-shipping harbour and a market for Far Eastern goods, paying tribute to Hormuz but running its own affairs. Its site is one of the largest medieval towns in the Emirates.
entries.note: Julfar / al-Mataf and al-Nudud excavations (Kennet; Sasaki; King); its role in the Hormuzi network.

entries.label: The pearl banks as the Jabrids' treasury
entries.loc: Bahrain and the eastern Arabian banks
entries.hint: Holding Bahrain gave the Jabrids the richest pearl fishery in the world. Pearl revenue, more than the thin taxes of the desert, financed a state that could protect the Hajj and field armies across half of Arabia.
entries.note: Portuguese estimates of Bahrain's pearl revenue (Barbosa; Albuquerque); the Jabrid economy (al-Jasir).

entries.label: Dates, dried fish and the staple trades
entries.loc: al-Hasa, the Batinah, the Omani interior
entries.hint: Beneath the luxury trades ran the bulk economy: al-Hasa and Omani dates shipped to India and the Gulf ports, dried sardines feeding both people and livestock along the Batinah, and the aflaj-watered grain of the interior. This is what most people actually lived on.
entries.note: Ibn Battuta on the 'fish-fed' animals of Qalhat and Zufar; the date and dried-fish trades in the medieval and early-modern Gulf.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The kamal and the compass rose, the ocean dhow, and an island that imported its water

entries.label: Codifying the science of navigation
entries.hint: Ibn Majid turned the pilots' oral craft into a written technology — tables, rules, verse mnemonics — that could be taught rather than only apprenticed. It was the Gulf's most sophisticated body of applied knowledge.
entries.note: Tibbetts (1971); Ibn Majid's didactic 'urjuzas' (versified sailing manuals).

entries.label: The ocean-going dhow of Julfar and Sur
entries.hint: Gulf shipyards built the large sewn- and later nailed-plank vessels — the baghlah and ghanjah types — that carried horses, dates and porcelain across the open ocean. The hull form and rig were refined over this period into the classic Gulf ocean trader.
entries.note: Agius, 'Classic Ships of Islam' (2008); the Gulf shipbuilding centres of Sur and the northern coast.

entries.label: Hormuz — a city that shipped in its water
entries.hint: The island had no fresh water, no crops and no grazing. Everything came by boat from the mainland and Qeshm; households stored water in great plastered cisterns, and wind-catching towers cooled the houses. It was an entirely engineered urban environment.
entries.note: Portuguese descriptions of Hormuz's cisterns and badgirs (wind-towers); the island's total dependence on imported supply (Barbosa).

entries.label: Bahla — earthen military architecture at scale
entries.hint: Building a fort and a twelve-kilometre town wall in mud-brick, and keeping them standing in a climate of flash floods, required constant skilled maintenance and a deep understanding of earthen construction — a technology as demanding in its way as stone.
entries.note: Bahla Fort conservation studies (UNESCO); Omani mud-brick building technique.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Zheng He's fleets at Hormuz, Ibn Battuta on the coast, and merchants of every nation

entries.label: The Ming treasure fleets call at Hormuz
entries.hint: Zheng He's vast fleets reached Hormuz on three voyages, the furthest west China's state navy ever sailed in force. Ma Huan's account marvels at the market — every good on earth, he says, could be had there. Then, after 1433, China stopped coming.
entries.note: Ma Huan, 'Yingya Shenglan' (1433), the Hormuz ('Hulumosi') chapter; the 4th, 5th and 7th Zheng He voyages.

entries.label: Ibn Battuta on the Gulf
entries.hint: The Moroccan traveller sailed the length of the Gulf, leaving the fullest medieval eyewitness account of Hormuz's wealth, Qalhat's mosque, the Omani coast's fish-fed flocks and the manners of its people. His 'Rihla' is a primary source for the whole region.
entries.note: Ibn Battuta, 'Rihla', the Gulf and Oman sections (trans. Gibb).

entries.label: Horses for cottons — the Gulf–India exchange
entries.hint: The horse fleets came back from India loaded with cotton cloth, rice, sugar, spices and gold. The trade tied the political fortunes of the Deccan and South Indian kingdoms — always short of cavalry — directly to the ports of the Gulf.
entries.note: Wassaf and Abd al-Razzaq on the horse-for-textiles exchange; the strategic dependence of Indian states on Gulf horses (Digby 1971).

entries.label: A city of many nations
entries.hint: Persian, Arab, Gujarati and Sindhi Hindu, Jewish and later Armenian merchant communities all lived and traded at Hormuz under a king who taxed them impartially. The island was a functioning cosmopolitan city-state.
entries.note: Barbosa and Portuguese accounts of the resident merchant 'nations' at Hormuz.

entries.label: Omani links to the Swahili coast endure
entries.hint: Omani and Hormuzi shipping kept working the East African coast, trading cloth and beads for gold, ivory and slaves and reinforcing the Arab-Persian element in the Swahili towns. Kilwa's medieval prosperity and Oman's were connected.
entries.note: Ibn Battuta at Kilwa (1331); the medieval Swahili gold trade (Horton & Middleton, 'The Swahili', 2000).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The Mongol collapse, Timur, the Ming withdrawal and the sails coming round Africa

entries.label: The Il-Khanate falls apart
entries.loc: Iran; consequences for the Gulf shore
entries.hint: The disintegration of the Mongol state in Iran removed the overlord Hormuz had balanced against and threw the northern Gulf shore into a scramble of local dynasties. Hormuz's island position let it profit from the chaos.
entries.note: The end of the Il-Khanate (1335–53); the succession of Injuids, Muzaffarids and others in Fars (Aubin 1953).

entries.label: Timur's empire and Timurid Persia
entries.loc: Samarkand; Fars and the Gulf shore
entries.hint: Timur's conquests brought Fars, and with it the overlordship of Hormuz, under a single power again. Hormuz kept its trade by tribute; the Timurid century was, for the Gulf, a period of managed dependence.
entries.note: Manz, 'The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane' (1989); the Timurid tributary relationship with Hormuz.

entries.label: China withdraws from the sea
entries.hint: After the seventh voyage the Ming court ended the treasure fleets and turned inward. The Gulf lost its most spectacular trading partner, and the western Indian Ocean was left to its own merchant shipping — until European fleets arrived instead.
entries.note: The end of the Zheng He voyages and the Ming maritime retrenchment (Dreyer, 'Zheng He', 2007).

entries.label: The Safavids seize Persia
entries.hint: Shah Ismail's founding of the Safavid state — militantly Twelver Shia — put an aggressive new power on the Gulf's northern shore just as the Portuguese appeared on its southern approaches. Hormuz would soon be caught between them.
entries.note: Ismail I's rise (Battle of Sharur, 1501); the Safavid claim to the Persian Gulf coast.

entries.label: The Portuguese round Africa
entries.hint: Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape in 1488 and Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498, guided across the Arabian Sea from Malindi by an Indian Ocean pilot. A sea route from Europe to the spice lands now existed — and it ran past the mouth of the Gulf.
entries.note: da Gama's 1498 voyage; the tradition (disputed) that his pilot from Malindi was Ahmad ibn Majid of Julfar — Tibbetts (1971) is sceptical.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: A woman ruling Qalhat, the slave market of Hormuz and the islanders who owned nothing but trade

entries.label: Bibi Maryam, lady of Qalhat
entries.hint: After her husband Ayaz, Hormuz's vizier and governor of Qalhat, died, Bibi Maryam ruled the port in her own right, kept it prosperous, and built the mausoleum that still bears her name. Ibn Battuta calls her 'a pious woman' and singles out her mosque as the town's finest building.
entries.note: Ibn Battuta, 'Rihla', Qalhat; Aubin (1953) on Ayaz and the Qalhat governorship.

entries.label: The slave market of Hormuz
entries.hint: Hormuz trafficked people from every shore it touched — East Africans, Indians, Circassians, Nubians — sold as domestic servants, concubines, pearl divers and soldiers. Slave-dealing was one of the ordinary businesses of the jewel of the world.
entries.note: Portuguese descriptions of the Hormuz slave trade (Barbosa; Albuquerque); the Indian Ocean slave routes (Alpers, 'The Indian Ocean in World History', 2014).

entries.label: An island population with no land
entries.hint: Hormuz's tens of thousands of inhabitants grew nothing and herded nothing; every mouthful of food and drop of water was bought. Their whole existence depended on the trade continuing to flow — which is why the Portuguese blockade of 1507 was a death sentence for the city.
entries.note: The island's total dependence on imported supply (Barbosa); the vulnerability that made Albuquerque's blockade decisive.

entries.label: Scholarly women of the Shia oases
entries.hint: In the learned families of al-Ahsa and Bahrain, women transmitted hadith, held ijazas (licences to teach) and copied manuscripts, their names surviving in the chains of transmission and the later biographical dictionaries. Female learning was part of how the tradition reproduced itself.
entries.note: Women in the transmission chains and biographical literature of the Bahrani Shia scholarly tradition (later collected in al-Bahrani, 'Lu'lu'at al-Bahrayn').
